sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, neglect, restraint and the deaths of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Group homes and other residential services for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track them. The people who live in them are adults, with a rights movement of their own led by self-advocates.

This page is about where that system meets the troubled teen industry. The two grew from the same institutions, some of the same companies run both, and the methods used to control teenagers were developed on disabled children.

We are not the experts on this system. The self-advocates and organizations listed below are.

sections.label: The same roots
sections.heading: The same roots
sections.body:
Both systems began in the institutions built to keep disabled people apart. The first opened on Randall's Island in New York in 1847 and in Massachusetts in 1848, at the school later called the Fernald Center, whose administrators included eugenicists. States sterilized people in their care, many of them adolescents, and in *Buck v. Bell* (1927) the Supreme Court upheld the sterilization of Carrie Buck, a teenager held at the Virginia Colony for Epileptics and Feeble-Minded ([developmental disabilities and eugenics](/idd-timeline/)). These institutions are among the roots of the troubled teen industry.

When the institutions emptied, both systems passed into private hands on the same money. The state institutions held 194,650 people at their peak in 1967.[^1] Deinstitutionalization began in the 1960s, underfunding left gaps that private providers filled, and from 1965 Medicaid let public money follow a person into a private placement, as it does for youth residential treatment ([the birth of the TTI](/birth-of-the-tti/)). Today private providers run almost every home for disabled adults outside a family's: of about 232,000, states run 1,940.[^1]

sections.label: The same companies
sections.heading: The same companies
sections.body:
Some of the same companies serve people on both sides of the age line.

Table: Companies in both systems
| Company | Adults with IDD | Youth programs |
|---|---|---|
| Sevita (The MENTOR Network) | 70,000 people served across its services[^2] | Foster care;[^2] NeuroRestorative's [14 group homes for young people in Illinois](/facility/neurorestorative-il/), in our records |
| BrightSpring (ResCare) | More than 600 residential facilities in 2019[^3] | Foster care and youth services;[^4] 2 West Virginia programs in our records |
| Devereux | More than 60 group homes in New Jersey,[^5] adult homes in Massachusetts[^6] | [43 programs in our records](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/), 12 for children with IDD[^7] |
| AdvoServ (Bellwether) | 62 group homes in New Jersey until 2019[^8] | A Delaware program in our records |
| Judge Rotenberg Center | Adults[^9] | Children; [in our records](/facility/judge-rotenberg-educational-center-ma/) |

A disabled child can grow up inside one of these companies. The Senate Finance Committee found Devereux stays of up to 6,928 days, almost 19 years, on its Florida campus.[^7]

Sevita's record crosses the age line. Private equity has owned it since 2001 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)). The Senate Finance Committee made its foster care the case study of a 2017 investigation of for-profit foster care,[^10] which raised concerns about treatment and deaths among foster children in its care.[^11] In 2020 the committee found "a consistent pattern of substandard care" at MENTOR Oregon's adult homes[^12][^13] and recurring critical incidents, including failures to report abuse or neglect, at REM Iowa.[^14] In 2024 Florida moved to revoke the license of its NeuroRestorative unit over its use of restraint and seclusion on children.[^15]

BrightSpring's record crosses it too. As ResCare it called itself the nation's largest private provider of services for people with developmental disabilities, and its youth division ran residential treatment for young people with emotional and behavioral issues and for juveniles in the justice system.[^16] After the private equity firm KKR took control in March 2019, its intermediate care facilities in seven states were 16 percent of the total but received 40 percent of the most serious citations, more than 500, through 2021, while the company paid more than $135 million a year in interest on its loans. KKR and BrightSpring disputed the findings.[^3]

So does AdvoServ's. Bought by Wellspring Capital Management in 2015,[^17] it renamed itself Bellwether Behavioral Health in 2017 after ProPublica reported the deaths of three teenagers in its care and its frequent use of restraints.[^18] Two years later New Jersey moved its adult group homes to other providers.[^8]

sections.label: The same methods
sections.heading: The same methods
sections.body:
Much of the behavior control used in troubled teen programs was developed on disabled children. In 1965 Ivar Lovaas published his use of electric shock on autistic children at UCLA. Applied Behavior Analysis, defined in 1968, was first used to enforce compliance in disabled and autistic children, and in 1971 Matthew Israel founded the Behavior Research Institute, now the Judge Rotenberg Center ([experimental group psychology](/experimental-group-psychology/)). Point systems, levels and punishment for "noncompliance" passed back and forth between these programs and the ones built for troubled teens.

The Judge Rotenberg Center in Canton, Massachusetts, uses the harshest of these methods on children and adults alike. It is the only facility in the country known to use electric skin shock on the people in its care; the FDA estimated that about 50 people had treatment plans that included it.[^19] The FDA banned the devices in 2020. A federal appeals court vacated the ban in July 2021, Congress gave the FDA clear authority in 2022, and the FDA proposed a new ban in March 2024.[^20] As of October 2026 no final rule had been published.

Where the two systems meet, people have died. A 19-year-old autistic resident died after a restraint at Laurel Heights, a Universal Health Services youth hospital in Georgia.[^7]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of adults with disabilities in most states. In some states a separate agency handles adults with developmental disabilities, or adults under 60. The National Adult Protective Services Association keeps [the reporting contact for every state and territory](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **The Eldercare Locator**, run by the federal government, refers callers to local agencies, mainly for older adults: call or text 1-800-677-1116, or visit [eldercare.acl.gov](https://eldercare.acl.gov/).
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies** are independent disability rights agencies in every state and territory. Find yours in the [National Disability Rights Network directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate abuse and neglect of residents of health care facilities and board and care facilities, and of Medicaid enrollees in other settings ([HHS Office of Inspector General](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/)).
- Also tell the state agency that licenses the home or pays for the services.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists agencies state by state.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [Self Advocates Becoming Empowered (SABE)](https://www.sabeusa.org/): The nationwide organization of self-advocates, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities speaking for themselves. Its priorities include closing institutions.
- [Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/): A national disability rights organization run by and for autistic people.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A grassroots disability rights group known for direct action for the right to live at home, not in nursing homes and institutions.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/about/): The membership organization for the Protection and Advocacy agencies and Client Assistance Programs in every state and territory.
- [The Arc of the United States](https://thearc.org/about-us/): Has advocated for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families since 1950, with chapters across the country.
- [National Council on Independent Living (NCIL)](https://www.ncil.org/about/): A cross-disability organization advocating for independent living and disability rights since 1982.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in this system, or you are a self-advocate or a family member, and something on this page is wrong, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
